title: CTS Unit 4 — The Gift of Tongues in the Book of Acts / El don de lenguas en Hechos

blocks.en: Pentecostalism & the Charismatic Movement · Unit 4
blocks.es_reference: El pentecostalismo y el movimiento carismático · Unidad 4

blocks.en: The Gift of Tongues in the Book of Acts
blocks.es_reference: El don de lenguas en el libro de Hechos

blocks.en: A Biblical Study · New King James Version
blocks.es_reference: Un estudio bíblico · Reina-Valera Gómez

blocks.en: “For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are afar off, as many as the Lord our God will call.”Acts 2:39 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “Porque para vosotros es la promesa, y para vuestros hijos, y para todos los que están lejos; para cuantos el Señor nuestro Dios llamare.”Hechos 2:39 (RVG)

blocks.en: Learning Objectives
blocks.es_reference: Objetivos de aprendizaje

blocks.en: By the end of this unit you should be able to:
blocks.es_reference: Al terminar esta unidad, usted debe poder:

blocks.en: Locate the four outpourings of the Spirit in Acts within the geographic movement of Acts 1:8.
blocks.es_reference: Ubicar los cuatro derramamientos del Espíritu en Hechos dentro del movimiento geográfico de Hechos 1:8.

blocks.en: Show, from the text, why the tongues of Pentecost were known human languages.
blocks.es_reference: Mostrar, desde el texto, por qué las lenguas de Pentecostés fueron idiomas humanos conocidos.

blocks.en: Distinguish describing what happened (narrative) from prescribing what all must do (command), and apply it to tongues in both directions.
blocks.es_reference: Distinguir el describir lo que sucedió (narrativa) del mandar lo que todos deben hacer (mandato), y aplicarlo a las lenguas en ambas direcciones.

blocks.en: Keep apart two questions: whether the gift is genuine, and whether tongues is the required initial evidence of a second blessing.
blocks.es_reference: Mantener separadas dos preguntas: si el don es genuino, y si las lenguas son la evidencia inicial requerida de una segunda bendición.

blocks.en: Explain a Christ-centered, charitable posture toward Pentecostal and charismatic believers.
blocks.es_reference: Explicar una postura centrada en Cristo y caritativa hacia los creyentes pentecostales y carismáticos.

blocks.en: One Event, or a Pattern for All?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Un solo suceso o un patrón para todos?

blocks.en: Acts chapter 2 records the first great outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the church. Because that day was so glorious, believers in every generation have asked a natural question: must every later work of the Spirit look exactly like Pentecost? Should the whole Christian life be measured against that single morning in Jerusalem?
blocks.es_reference: El capítulo 2 de Hechos registra el primer gran derramamiento del Espíritu Santo sobre la iglesia. Por ser aquel día tan glorioso, los creyentes de cada generación se han hecho una pregunta natural: ¿debe toda obra posterior del Espíritu parecerse exactamente a Pentecostés? ¿Ha de medirse toda la vida cristiana por aquella sola mañana en Jerusalén?

blocks.en: Luke, who wrote Acts, does not leave us to guess. Rather than closing the story in Jerusalem, he records three more occasions on which the Holy Spirit came upon a new group of believers: the Samaritans (Acts 8), the household of the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10), and a small band of John the Baptist's disciples at Ephesus (Acts 19). These four accounts have stood at the center of every discussion about Spirit baptism and speaking in tongues. Some believers read them as a fixed pattern that every Christian should repeat. Others read them as milestones in the spread of the gospel during the apostolic age. Before we choose between these readings, we must do what we always do: ask what Luke himself intended to teach.
blocks.es_reference: Lucas, quien escribió Hechos, no nos deja adivinar. En lugar de cerrar la historia en Jerusalén, registra tres ocasiones más en que el Espíritu Santo vino sobre un nuevo grupo de creyentes: los samaritanos (Hechos 8), la casa del gentil Cornelio (Hechos 10) y un pequeño grupo de discípulos de Juan el Bautista en Éfeso (Hechos 19). Estos cuatro relatos han estado en el centro de toda discusión sobre el bautismo del Espíritu y el hablar en lenguas. Algunos creyentes los leen como un patrón fijo que todo cristiano debe repetir. Otros los leen como hitos en la expansión del evangelio durante la era apostólica. Antes de elegir entre estas lecturas, debemos hacer lo que siempre hacemos: preguntar qué quiso enseñar el propio Lucas.

blocks.en: The Map Luke Gave Us: Acts 1:8
blocks.es_reference: El mapa que Lucas nos dio: Hechos 1:8

blocks.en: Just before His ascension, the Lord Jesus told His disciples:
blocks.es_reference: Poco antes de ascender, el Señor Jesús dijo a sus discípulos:

blocks.en: “But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be witnesses to Me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”Acts 1:8 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “Pero recibiréis poder cuando haya venido sobre vosotros el Espíritu Santo; y me seréis testigos en Jerusalén, en toda Judea, en Samaria, y hasta lo último de la tierra.”Hechos 1:8 (RVG)

blocks.en: That single verse is the map of the entire book. The gospel moves outward in stages — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the Gentile world, until at last it reaches Rome itself, the heart of the empire. Each major advance carries the same message: God is not building many separate churches but one church, made of Jews and Gentiles together. And at each frontier, the coming of the Spirit upon a new people is God's own public seal that He has received them into the body of Christ. This missionary movement is the frame around which every scene in Acts is arranged. Keep that map before you, and the four outpourings begin to make sense.
blocks.es_reference: Ese solo versículo es el mapa de todo el libro. El evangelio avanza hacia afuera por etapas: Jerusalén, luego Judea y Samaria, después el mundo gentil, hasta llegar por fin a Roma misma, el corazón del imperio. Cada gran avance lleva el mismo mensaje: Dios no está edificando muchas iglesias separadas, sino una sola iglesia, formada por judíos y gentiles juntos. Y en cada frontera, la venida del Espíritu sobre un nuevo pueblo es el sello público del propio Dios de que los ha recibido en el cuerpo de Cristo. Este movimiento misionero es el marco alrededor del cual se ordena cada escena de Hechos. Tenga presente ese mapa, y los cuatro derramamientos comenzarán a cobrar sentido.

blocks.en: Pentecost Was Spoken in Known Languages
blocks.es_reference: Pentecostés se habló en lenguas conocidas

blocks.en: Here we must be careful and exact, because much confusion begins at this point. What kind of tongues were spoken on the day of Pentecost? Luke tells us plainly. When the sound drew a crowd of Jewish pilgrims from many nations, they were bewildered —
blocks.es_reference: Aquí debemos ser cuidadosos y precisos, porque mucha confusión comienza en este punto. ¿Qué clase de lenguas se hablaron en el día de Pentecostés? Lucas nos lo dice con claridad. Cuando el estruendo reunió a una multitud de peregrinos judíos de muchas naciones, quedaron confusos —

blocks.en: “…because everyone heard them speak in his own language.”  And they marveled, “…how is it that we hear, each in our own language in which we were born?”Acts 2:6, 8 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “…porque cada uno les oía hablar en su propia lengua.”  Y, maravillados, decían: “…¿cómo les oímos nosotros hablar cada uno en nuestra lengua en la que hemos nacido?”Hechos 2:6, 8 (RVG)

blocks.en: The miracle of Pentecost was not unintelligible speech. It was the very opposite: Galileans praising God in the native languages of Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and a dozen other peoples who had never taught them a word.
blocks.es_reference: El milagro de Pentecostés no fue un hablar ininteligible. Fue todo lo contrario: galileos alabando a Dios en los idiomas nativos de partos, medos, elamitas y una docena de otros pueblos que jamás les habían enseñado una palabra.

blocks.en: This matters. At Babel (Genesis 11), God had scattered humanity by confusing their language. At Pentecost He began to gather the nations back by giving His disciples their languages. Pentecost was a sign that the gospel would cross every barrier of tongue and nation. Whatever the word “tongues” may mean in other passages, at Pentecost itself the tongues were real, known, human languages. For that reason it is a stretch to treat Pentecost as the model of an unknown, ecstatic tongue. The text points the other way.
blocks.es_reference: Esto importa. En Babel (Génesis 11), Dios había dispersado a la humanidad confundiendo su lengua. En Pentecostés comenzó a reunir de nuevo a las naciones dando a sus discípulos los idiomas de ellas. Pentecostés fue señal de que el evangelio cruzaría toda barrera de lengua y de nación. Cualquiera que sea el significado de la palabra “lenguas” en otros pasajes, en Pentecostés mismo las lenguas eran idiomas humanos reales y conocidos. Por esa razón es exagerado tratar Pentecostés como el modelo de una lengua desconocida o extática. El texto apunta en la dirección contraria.

blocks.en: Acts 8 — The Samaritans
blocks.es_reference: Hechos 8 — Los samaritanos

blocks.en: The first great leap outward was into Samaria. For centuries Jews and Samaritans had lived in bitter division. When persecution scattered the Jerusalem believers, Philip went down to Samaria and preached Christ, and the results were wonderful: many believed, many were baptized, and there was great joy in the city.
blocks.es_reference: El primer gran salto hacia afuera fue hacia Samaria. Durante siglos, judíos y samaritanos habían vivido en amarga división. Cuando la persecución dispersó a los creyentes de Jerusalén, Felipe descendió a Samaria y predicó a Cristo, y los resultados fueron admirables: muchos creyeron, muchos fueron bautizados y hubo gran gozo en la ciudad.

blocks.en: Yet something unusual happened. The Holy Spirit had not yet fallen on these new believers in the visible way seen in Jerusalem. So the apostles Peter and John came from Jerusalem, prayed for them, laid their hands on them, and then the Spirit was given. Luke does not actually say that the Samaritans spoke in tongues. Some think they must have, because Simon the sorcerer saw something so striking that he tried to buy the apostles' power with money. Others note that Luke deliberately leaves the details unspoken. Either way, one thing was made unmistakable to everyone present: God had received the Samaritans.
blocks.es_reference: Sin embargo, ocurrió algo inusual. El Espíritu Santo aún no había caído sobre estos nuevos creyentes de la manera visible que se vio en Jerusalén. Por eso los apóstoles Pedro y Juan vinieron de Jerusalén, oraron por ellos, les impusieron las manos, y entonces fue dado el Espíritu. Lucas en realidad no dice que los samaritanos hablaran en lenguas. Algunos piensan que debieron hacerlo, porque Simón el mago vio algo tan asombroso que intentó comprar con dinero el poder de los apóstoles. Otros notan que Lucas deja los detalles deliberadamente sin decir. De una u otra manera, una cosa quedó inconfundible para todos los presentes: Dios había recibido a los samaritanos.

blocks.en: Why the delay? Most likely for the sake of unity. Had the Samaritans received the Spirit entirely apart from the Jerusalem church, two rival churches might have formed — one Jewish, one Samaritan — repeating the old division inside the body of Christ. Instead, the apostles themselves witnessed and welcomed the Samaritans, and the church remained one under one Lord.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué la demora? Muy probablemente por causa de la unidad. Si los samaritanos hubieran recibido el Espíritu enteramente aparte de la iglesia de Jerusalén, podrían haberse formado dos iglesias rivales —una judía y otra samaritana—, repitiendo la vieja división dentro del cuerpo de Cristo. En cambio, los apóstoles mismos vieron y dieron la bienvenida a los samaritanos, y la iglesia permaneció una sola bajo un solo Señor.

blocks.en: Acts 10 — Cornelius and the Gentiles
blocks.es_reference: Hechos 10 — Cornelio y los gentiles

blocks.en: The next step was greater still. Cornelius was not a Samaritan; he was a Gentile, a Roman centurion. To many Jewish believers, the idea that uncircumcised Gentiles could enter God's covenant people without first becoming Jews was almost unthinkable. So God prepared Peter with a vision, teaching him to call no man unclean. Peter entered the Gentile's house and began to preach — and before the sermon was even finished, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard. Luke tells us the Jewish believers knew it —
blocks.es_reference: El siguiente paso fue aún mayor. Cornelio no era samaritano; era gentil, un centurión romano. Para muchos creyentes judíos, la idea de que gentiles incircuncisos pudieran entrar en el pueblo del pacto de Dios sin hacerse antes judíos era casi impensable. Por eso Dios preparó a Pedro con una visión, enseñándole a no llamar inmundo a ningún hombre. Pedro entró en la casa del gentil y comenzó a predicar, y antes de que el sermón terminara, el Espíritu Santo cayó sobre todos los que oían. Lucas nos dice que los creyentes judíos lo supieron —

blocks.en: “For they heard them speak with tongues and magnify God.”Acts 10:46 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “Porque los oían que hablaban en lenguas, y que magnificaban a Dios.”Hechos 10:46 (RVG)

blocks.en: Here the tongues served an unmistakable purpose. They proved to astonished Jewish Christians that God had accepted Gentiles on exactly the same footing as themselves — by grace, through faith, apart from the law. Later, when Peter was challenged in Jerusalem, this was his defense: God Himself had given them the same gift, so who was Peter to stand in God's way? Notice again that Luke does not tell us whether these tongues were known languages or something else. On that point we may hold our conclusion loosely; the text simply does not say.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí las lenguas sirvieron a un propósito inconfundible. Probaron a los asombrados cristianos judíos que Dios había aceptado a los gentiles exactamente sobre la misma base que a ellos: por gracia, mediante la fe, aparte de la ley. Más tarde, cuando Pedro fue cuestionado en Jerusalén, esta fue su defensa: Dios mismo les había dado el mismo don, ¿quién era Pedro para estorbar a Dios? Note de nuevo que Lucas no nos dice si estas lenguas eran idiomas conocidos o alguna otra cosa. Sobre ese punto podemos sostener nuestra conclusión sin apretarla; el texto sencillamente no lo dice.

blocks.en: Acts 19 — The Disciples at Ephesus
blocks.es_reference: Hechos 19 — Los discípulos en Éfeso

blocks.en: The last account is at Ephesus, where Paul met about twelve men who had received only John's baptism and had not so much as heard that the Holy Spirit had been given. Theirs was an unusual case: they were disciples of John the Baptist, living after the resurrection, who had never heard the completed gospel. Paul explained that John had pointed forward to Jesus; the men believed and were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; Paul laid hands on them —
blocks.es_reference: El último relato está en Éfeso, donde Pablo encontró a unos doce hombres que sólo habían recibido el bautismo de Juan y ni siquiera habían oído que se hubiese dado el Espíritu Santo. El suyo era un caso singular: eran discípulos de Juan el Bautista, viviendo después de la resurrección, que nunca habían oído el evangelio completo. Pablo les explicó que Juan había señalado hacia Jesús; los hombres creyeron y fueron bautizados en el nombre del Señor Jesús; Pablo les impuso las manos —

blocks.en: “…and they spoke with tongues and prophesied.”Acts 19:6 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “…y hablaban en lenguas, y profetizaban.”Hechos 19:6 (RVG)

blocks.en: Once more, God openly confirmed that another group had been brought into the new-covenant people of Christ.
blocks.es_reference: Una vez más, Dios confirmó abiertamente que otro grupo había sido introducido en el pueblo del nuevo pacto de Cristo.

blocks.en: Four Scenes, One Author's Purpose
blocks.es_reference: Cuatro escenas, un propósito del autor

blocks.en: Set the four accounts side by side and both their unity and their variety stand out. In every case the Holy Spirit works, the gospel advances to new people, and God — not man — takes the initiative. Yet the circumstances differ sharply. At Pentecost the Spirit came with no laying on of hands. In Samaria He came through the apostles' hands. In Cornelius's house He came while Peter was still preaching, before baptism. At Ephesus He came after baptism and the laying on of hands. There is no fixed sequence here that every believer must pass through. It is worth noticing, too, that Luke reports tongues explicitly at only some of these outpourings — at Pentecost, at Cornelius's house, and at Ephesus — while in Samaria he never mentions them at all. Even the most-discussed sign, then, is not made to appear at every step, and that single observation should make us cautious about turning any one scene into a rule that binds every believer for all time. What Luke shows us is not a formula but the sovereign freedom of God, opening the door of faith to one people after another.
blocks.es_reference: Coloque los cuatro relatos lado a lado y resaltarán tanto su unidad como su variedad. En cada caso el Espíritu Santo obra, el evangelio avanza a un nuevo pueblo, y Dios —no el hombre— toma la iniciativa. Sin embargo, las circunstancias difieren notablemente. En Pentecostés el Espíritu vino sin imposición de manos. En Samaria vino por medio de las manos de los apóstoles. En la casa de Cornelio vino mientras Pedro aún predicaba, antes del bautismo. En Éfeso vino después del bautismo y la imposición de manos. No hay aquí una secuencia fija por la que todo creyente deba pasar. Vale la pena notar también que Lucas menciona expresamente las lenguas solo en algunos de estos derramamientos —en Pentecostés, en la casa de Cornelio y en Éfeso—, mientras que en Samaria no las menciona en absoluto. Así que ni siquiera la señal más debatida aparece en cada paso, y esa sola observación debería hacernos cautelosos antes de convertir una escena cualquiera en una regla que obligue a todo creyente para siempre. Lo que Lucas nos muestra no es una fórmula, sino la libertad soberana de Dios, que abre la puerta de la fe a un pueblo tras otro.

blocks.en: Describing Is Not the Same as Commanding
blocks.es_reference: Describir no es lo mismo que mandar

blocks.en: This brings us to a principle that guards us from many errors. The book of Acts is, first of all, history — a narrative of what happened. A narrative describes events; it does not automatically command us to repeat them. Acts describes believers selling their possessions, choosing an apostle by lot, being carried away by the Spirit, and being freed from prison by angels, yet the church has never taught that each of these must happen to every Christian. This takes nothing away from Scripture's authority. It simply reminds us to ask, in each passage, whether we are being shown what once occurred or being taught what must always be done.
blocks.es_reference: Esto nos lleva a un principio que nos guarda de muchos errores. El libro de Hechos es, ante todo, historia: un relato de lo que sucedió. Un relato describe sucesos; no nos manda automáticamente repetirlos. Hechos describe a creyentes que vendían sus posesiones, que echaban suertes para elegir a un apóstol, que eran arrebatados por el Espíritu, y que eran librados de la cárcel por ángeles; sin embargo, la iglesia nunca ha enseñado que cada una de estas cosas deba sucederle a todo cristiano. Esto no quita nada a la autoridad de la Escritura. Sólo nos recuerda preguntar, en cada pasaje, si se nos está mostrando lo que una vez ocurrió o enseñando lo que siempre debe hacerse.

blocks.en: That distinction is decisive for the subject of tongues, and it cuts in two directions at once. On one hand, because the four outpourings differ so widely, we should not build from them a single required pattern — as if every believer must have a second, separate experience marked by tongues. On the other hand, the same principle warns us not to rush to the opposite error of declaring the gift invalid. The narrative of Acts was never meant to settle, by itself, how the gifts function in the ordinary life of the church. For that we must turn to the passages that were written to teach the church directly — the letters of Paul.
blocks.es_reference: Esa distinción es decisiva para el tema de las lenguas, y corta en dos direcciones a la vez. Por un lado, como los cuatro derramamientos difieren tan ampliamente, no debemos construir a partir de ellos un solo patrón obligatorio, como si todo creyente debiera tener una segunda experiencia separada, señalada por las lenguas. Por otro lado, el mismo principio nos advierte que no corramos al error opuesto de declarar inválido el don. El relato de Hechos nunca fue escrito para definir, por sí solo, cómo funcionan los dones en la vida ordinaria de la iglesia. Para eso debemos volvernos a los pasajes que fueron escritos para enseñar directamente a la iglesia: las cartas de Pablo.

blocks.en: Two Questions We Must Keep Apart
blocks.es_reference: Dos preguntas que debemos mantener separadas

blocks.en: Much heat in this debate comes from confusing two very different questions. Let us hold them apart.
blocks.es_reference: Mucho del calor de este debate proviene de confundir dos preguntas muy distintas. Mantengámoslas separadas.

blocks.en: Question One — Answer: Yes
blocks.es_reference: Pregunta uno — Respuesta: Sí

blocks.en: Is the gift of tongues real and available?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Es el don de lenguas real y está disponible?

blocks.en: The epistles answer plainly. Paul does not deny the gift; he regulates it, thanks God for it in his own life, and tells the church, “do not forbid to speak with tongues” (1 Cor 14:39). A gift the church is commanded not to forbid is not a gift the church may declare extinct. The gift stands.
blocks.es_reference: Las epístolas responden con claridad. Pablo no niega el don; lo regula, da gracias a Dios por él en su propia vida, y manda a la iglesia: “no impidáis el hablar lenguas” (1 Cor 14:39). Un don que a la iglesia se le manda no prohibir no es un don que la iglesia pueda declarar extinto. El don permanece.

blocks.en: Question Two — Answer: No universal rule
blocks.es_reference: Pregunta dos — Respuesta: No hay regla universal

blocks.en: Is tongues the required initial evidence of a second blessing every believer must have?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Son las lenguas la evidencia inicial requerida de una segunda bendición que todo creyente debe recibir?

blocks.en: Here Acts gives no universal rule. The four accounts vary too much to yield one, and the great majority of believers in Acts are never said to speak in tongues at all. We decline the required-evidence doctrine while gladly affirming the gift itself.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí Hechos no da ninguna regla universal. Los cuatro relatos varían demasiado para producir una, y de la gran mayoría de los creyentes en Hechos nunca se dice que hablaran en lenguas. Rechazamos la doctrina de la evidencia requerida, mientras afirmamos con gozo el don mismo.

blocks.en: We can therefore hold two truths together without contradiction: the gift is genuine, and yet tongues is not the mandatory proof that must accompany every true reception of the Spirit. To affirm the first while declining the second is not a compromise; it is simply following the text where it leads.
blocks.es_reference: Podemos, por tanto, sostener juntas dos verdades sin contradicción: el don es genuino, y sin embargo las lenguas no son la prueba obligatoria que deba acompañar toda verdadera recepción del Espíritu. Afirmar lo primero y a la vez rechazar lo segundo no es un arreglo; es sencillamente seguir el texto adonde conduce.

blocks.en: The Fruit We Cannot Deny
blocks.es_reference: El fruto que no podemos negar

blocks.en: Whatever our conclusions on these fine points, honesty compels us to reckon with what God has done through Spirit-filled believers in our own age. Today roughly 644 million Christians — about one in four believers on earth — belong to the Pentecostal and charismatic movement, and for more than a hundred years these Christians have stood at the very front of world evangelism, carrying the gospel into places others never reached. We may weigh doctrines carefully, and we will; but we cannot look at that harvest and fail to give thanks. Where Christ is preached and sinners are saved, the Holy Spirit is at work.
blocks.es_reference: Cualesquiera que sean nuestras conclusiones sobre estos puntos finos, la honestidad nos obliga a considerar lo que Dios ha hecho por medio de creyentes llenos del Espíritu en nuestra propia época. Hoy alrededor de 644 millones de cristianos —cerca de uno de cada cuatro creyentes en la tierra— pertenecen al movimiento pentecostal y carismático, y por más de cien años estos cristianos han estado al frente mismo de la evangelización mundial, llevando el evangelio a lugares que otros nunca alcanzaron. Podemos sopesar las doctrinas con cuidado, y lo haremos; pero no podemos mirar esa cosecha y dejar de dar gracias. Donde Cristo es predicado y los pecadores son salvos, el Espíritu Santo está obrando.

blocks.en: A word of caution. The prosperity gospel — the promise that faith guarantees health and wealth — often travels alongside charismatic preaching, but it is not the same thing, and it should never be treated as if it were. We will examine it on its own in a later unit. Classical Pentecostal and charismatic believers are not to be judged by that distortion; the movement must be weighed by Scripture, not by its worst excesses.
blocks.es_reference: Una palabra de cautela. El evangelio de la prosperidad —la promesa de que la fe garantiza salud y riqueza— a menudo viaja junto a la predicación carismática, pero no es lo mismo, y nunca debe tratarse como si lo fuera. Lo examinaremos por sí solo en una unidad posterior. Los creyentes pentecostales y carismáticos clásicos no han de ser juzgados por esa distorsión; el movimiento debe pesarse por la Escritura, no por sus peores excesos.

blocks.en: Christ at the Center
blocks.es_reference: Cristo en el centro

blocks.en: The Lord Jesus said that when the Spirit came, He would glorify Christ (John 16:14). That is the test of every gift and every movement. Tongues, healing, prophecy, teaching — all of them are given not to exalt an experience or a man, but to lift up the Savior and build His body in love. So we come to our Pentecostal and charismatic brothers and sisters not as opponents to be defeated but as family in Christ, holding fast to Scripture, testing all things, and keeping the Lord Jesus at the center of all.
blocks.es_reference: El Señor Jesús dijo que cuando el Espíritu viniera, Él glorificaría a Cristo (Juan 16:14). Esa es la prueba de todo don y de todo movimiento. Las lenguas, la sanidad, la profecía, la enseñanza: todo es dado no para exaltar una experiencia ni a un hombre, sino para levantar al Salvador y edificar su cuerpo en amor. Así nos acercamos a nuestros hermanos pentecostales y carismáticos no como adversarios a quienes vencer, sino como familia en Cristo, aferrándonos a la Escritura, probándolo todo y manteniendo al Señor Jesús en el centro de todo.

blocks.en: Looking Ahead
blocks.es_reference: Mirando adelante

blocks.en: In the next unit we turn from the narrative of Acts to the direct teaching of Paul in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12–14, and Ephesians 4. There we will find that the apostle's deepest concern is not which gifts a believer possesses, but whether every gift is used in love, in order, and for the building up of the body of Christ.
blocks.es_reference: En la próxima unidad pasaremos del relato de Hechos a la enseñanza directa de Pablo en Romanos 12, 1 Corintios 12–14 y Efesios 4. Allí descubriremos que la más honda preocupación del apóstol no es cuáles dones posee un creyente, sino si cada don se usa en amor, en orden y para la edificación del cuerpo de Cristo.

blocks.en: Discussion Questions
blocks.es_reference: Preguntas para discusión

blocks.en: How does keeping Acts 1:8 in view change the way we read the four outpourings of the Spirit?

mc.stem: On the day of Pentecost, the tongues that were spoken were —
options: known human languages the pilgrims recognized
an unknown, ecstatic prayer language
understood only by the apostles
written, not spoken
mc.why: The crowd heard their own native languages (Acts 2:6, 8). Pentecost was a reversal of Babel, not ecstatic speech.

mc.stem: Acts 1:8 functions in the book as —
options: a warning against missions
a promise fulfilled only at Pentecost
the geographic outline of the whole book
a command to remain in Jerusalem forever
mc.why: Jerusalem → Judea and Samaria → the ends of the earth maps the entire narrative of Acts.

mc.stem: In Acts 8, concerning the Samaritans, Luke —
options: explicitly says they spoke in tongues
does not actually state that they spoke in tongues
says they refused the Spirit
records no response at all
mc.why: Luke leaves it unstated. Something visible happened (Simon's reaction), but tongues are never named.

mc.stem: The most likely reason the Spirit's coming was delayed in Samaria until the apostles arrived was —
options: to punish the Samaritans
because Philip lacked faith
because tongues are always required first
to preserve the unity of the one church
mc.why: Apostolic witness kept Jewish and Samaritan believers one church rather than two rival bodies.

mc.stem: In the house of Cornelius (Acts 10), the tongues chiefly served to —
options: show the Gentiles were superior
prove God accepted Gentiles by faith on the same footing as Jews
replace the preaching of the gospel
begin a new law for Gentiles
mc.why: The sign convinced Jewish believers; Peter later appealed to it to defend Gentile inclusion.

mc.stem: The principle that Acts “describes” rather than automatically “prescribes” means that —
options: we should not build a universal required pattern from varied narratives, and also should not declare the gift invalid
the events in Acts are untrue
we may ignore the book of Acts
tongues have certainly ceased
mc.why: The principle cuts both ways. How the gifts function in church life is settled by the epistles, not by narrative alone.

mc.stem: A biblically balanced conclusion from this unit is that —
options: tongues is the required initial evidence for every believer
the gift of tongues is invalid today
the gift is genuine, yet tongues is not the mandatory proof of receiving the Spirit
Pentecostals are not true Christians
mc.why: Affirm the gift; decline the required-evidence doctrine; receive fellow believers as family in Christ.

sa.prompt: Explain why it is a stretch to treat the tongues of Pentecost (Acts 2) as an unknown or ecstatic tongue.
sa.model: At Pentecost the crowd heard the disciples praising God in their own native languages, so the tongues were real, known human languages, not unintelligible speech. This was a reversal of Babel, gathering the nations by giving the disciples their languages. Because everyone understood, it is a stretch to read Pentecost as an unknown or ecstatic tongue.

sa.prompt: Distinguish the two questions the Pentecostal movement raises about tongues, and state how you would answer each from Scripture.
sa.model: The first question is whether the gift of tongues is real and available; Scripture answers yes, since Paul regulates tongues and tells the church not to forbid them. The second question is whether tongues is the required initial evidence of a second blessing every believer must have; Acts gives no universal rule, since the accounts vary and most believers never speak in tongues. So we affirm the gift while declining the required evidence.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between description and prescription in Acts, and how it applies to tongues in both directions.
sa.model: Acts is narrative; it describes what happened but does not automatically command every believer to repeat it. This cuts two ways for tongues: we should not build a required pattern from the varied outpourings, yet we also must not declare the gift invalid, since narrative was not written to settle how gifts function. For that teaching we turn to the epistles.

sa.prompt: Name the four outpourings of the Spirit in Acts and explain how Acts 1:8 frames them.
sa.model: Pentecost in Jerusalem (Acts 2), the Samaritans (Acts 8), the household of the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10), and the disciples of John at Ephesus (Acts 19). Acts 1:8 is the map of the book: the gospel moves outward in stages, Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, then the Gentile world, until it reaches Rome. Each advance carries the message that God is building one church of Jews and Gentiles, and at each frontier the coming of the Spirit on a new people is God's public seal that He has received them into the body of Christ.

sa.prompt: What happened in Samaria in Acts 8, and why was the Spirit's coming most likely delayed until the apostles arrived?
sa.model: Philip preached Christ in Samaria; many believed and were baptized and there was great joy, yet the Spirit had not yet fallen visibly, so Peter and John came from Jerusalem, prayed, laid hands on them, and the Spirit was given. Luke does not actually say the Samaritans spoke in tongues, though Simon the sorcerer saw something striking enough to try to buy the power. The delay was most likely for unity: had the Samaritans received the Spirit apart from the Jerusalem church, two rival churches, Jewish and Samaritan, might have formed; instead the apostles themselves witnessed and welcomed them, and the church remained one.

sa.prompt: What did the tongues in Cornelius's house prove, and how did Peter later use it in his defense?
sa.model: Cornelius was a Gentile Roman centurion, and to many Jewish believers the idea of uncircumcised Gentiles entering the covenant without becoming Jews was almost unthinkable; God prepared Peter with a vision to call no man unclean. Before the sermon was finished the Spirit fell on all who heard, and the Jewish believers heard them speak with tongues and magnify God. The tongues proved that God had accepted Gentiles on exactly the same footing, by grace through faith apart from the law; when challenged in Jerusalem, Peter's defense was that God Himself had given them the same gift, so who was he to stand in God's way. Luke does not say whether these tongues were known languages.

sa.prompt: Compare the circumstances of the four outpourings and explain what that variety teaches.
sa.model: At Pentecost the Spirit came with no laying on of hands; in Samaria through the apostles' hands; in Cornelius's house while Peter was still preaching, before baptism; at Ephesus after baptism and the laying on of hands. There is no fixed sequence every believer must pass through, and Luke reports tongues explicitly at only some of the outpourings, never in Samaria, so even the most-discussed sign is not made to appear at every step. That should make us cautious about turning any one scene into a rule binding every believer; Luke shows not a formula but the sovereign freedom of God opening the door of faith to one people after another.

sa.prompt: Give examples from Acts that show why a narrative does not automatically command us to repeat it.
sa.model: Acts is first of all history, a narrative of what happened, and a narrative describes events without automatically commanding us to repeat them. Acts describes believers selling their possessions, choosing an apostle by lot, Philip being carried away by the Spirit, and prisoners freed by angels, yet the church has never taught that each must happen to every Christian. This takes nothing from Scripture's authority; it reminds us to ask in each passage whether we are being shown what once occurred or taught what must always be done.

sa.prompt: How does 1 Corinthians 14:39 answer the question whether the gift of tongues is real, and why does Acts give no universal rule on initial evidence?
sa.model: Paul does not deny the gift; he regulates it, thanks God for it in his own life, and tells the church, 'do not forbid to speak with tongues' (1 Corinthians 14:39). A gift the church is commanded not to forbid is not a gift the church may declare extinct, so the gift stands. On initial evidence Acts gives no universal rule: the four accounts vary too much to yield one, and the great majority of believers in Acts are never said to speak in tongues at all. The course declines the required-evidence doctrine while affirming the gift itself, and that is not a compromise but following the text where it leads.

sa.prompt: What 'fruit we cannot deny' does the unit acknowledge, and what caution does it attach about the prosperity gospel?
sa.model: Roughly 644 million Christians, about one in four believers on earth, belong to the Pentecostal and charismatic movement, and for more than a hundred years they have stood at the front of world evangelism, carrying the gospel where others never reached; we may weigh doctrines carefully, but we cannot look at that harvest and fail to give thanks, for where Christ is preached and sinners saved the Spirit is at work. The prosperity gospel, the promise that faith guarantees health and wealth, often travels alongside charismatic preaching but is not the same thing; classical Pentecostal and charismatic believers are not to be judged by that distortion, and the movement must be weighed by Scripture, not by its worst excesses.
